steps: Sort a short unsorted array and print it.
Ask for the argsort positions of the same array.
Walk the positions back through the source to confirm the order.
sort and argsort.realWorld: Reordering a names array by the scores array needs positions, not values, so argsort is the call that keeps the two columns aligned.
mistakes: Sorting the scores and forgetting the names now point at nothing.
Assuming argsort returns the sorted values.
revision: sort returns values; argsort returns the positions that would sort it.
Feed argsort's output into the parallel array to reorder it in step.

steps: Take an array that is already sorted.
Ask where a missing value would be inserted.
Print the index and check the neighbours around it.
searchsorted.realWorld: Mapping values into buckets — age bands, price tiers — is a binary search over sorted edges rather than a scan per record.
mistakes: Calling it on an unsorted array and trusting the meaningless index.
Forgetting the default side='left' decides where ties land.
revision: searchsorted assumes sorted input and returns an insertion index.
The result is a position, so it indexes the edges array.

steps: Get the distinct values of an array with repeats.
Ask which values the two arrays share.
Compare the shapes and confirm the output is sorted.
Unique values and set operations.realWorld: Reconciling two customer lists — who is in both, who is only in one — is a set operation instead of a nested membership loop.
mistakes: Expecting the original order; unique always sorts.
Using a Python set comprehension on a large array and losing the speed.
revision: unique returns sorted distinct values.
intersect1d, union1d and setdiff1d are the set questions.

steps: Sort a 2×3 matrix along axis 1.
Print the result and confirm each row is independently ordered.
Repeat with axis=0 and see the columns sorted instead.
sort each row separately.realWorld: Sorting each sample's readings while keeping the samples in place is a row sort; axis=0 would destroy the record boundaries.
mistakes: Using the default axis on a matrix and flattening the structure.
Assuming rows move relative to each other.
revision: axis=1 sorts inside each row.
axis=0 sorts down each column instead.

steps: Sort ascending.
Reverse the sorted result with a negative step.
Confirm the largest value is now first.
Reverse a sorted array for descending or.realWorld: Leaderboards and top-N reports present descending order, which takes a sort plus one reversal slice.
mistakes: Reversing before sorting and calling it descending.
Assuming there is a descending flag on np.sort.
revision: NumPy sorts ascending only.
Descending is the reverse slice of the sorted result.

steps: Partition an array at position 2.
Print the first three values and confirm they are the three smallest.
Note the two halves are not internally sorted.
partition keeps only k small values in f.realWorld: Top-k selection — the three cheapest products, the five slowest requests — does not need a full sort, and partition is the cheaper call.
mistakes: Expecting the whole array to come back sorted.
Using partition when the full order is actually needed.
revision: Only the k-th position is guaranteed.
The elements on each side are unordered.

steps: Build a primary and a secondary key.
Pass the secondary key first and the primary last.
Apply the returned order to both columns.
lexsort orders by the last key first.realWorld: Sorting a report by date and then by amount inside each date is a two-key lexsort, with no tuple building.
mistakes: Passing the keys in the intuitive but wrong order.
Forgetting the output is a permutation, not sorted values.
revision: The LAST key in the tuple is the primary key.
The result indexes the data like argsort.

steps: Find the position of the largest value.
Use that index to fetch the label or row behind it.
Add an axis to get one best position per row.
argmax finds the best position.realWorld: A classifier's predicted class is argmax over the class scores; the value itself is never the answer the user wants.
mistakes: Reporting the maximum value instead of the class it belongs to.
Forgetting ties resolve to the FIRST occurrence.
revision: argmax returns an index, not a value.
It is the bridge from scores to labels.

steps: Sort positions rather than values.
Print the permutation.
Index a second array with it to reorder both together.
argsort returns the order, not the value.realWorld: Sorting a table by one column means carrying every other column along, and argsort is the only output that allows that.
mistakes: Using sort and losing the link to the other columns.
Applying the permutation to the already-sorted array.
revision: argsort returns positions that would sort the array.
Applying them to the source is what reorders the table.

steps: Call the array method instead of the function.
Note that it returns None.
Print the array to see it reordered.
sort can work in place.realWorld: Sorting a large array a program already owns in place avoids a second copy of the buffer.
mistakes: Assigning the return value and getting None.
Calling the method on a view and reordering the source as a side effect.
revision: ndarray.sort rearranges in place and returns None.
np.sort returns a new array.

steps: Pass an unsorted array with repeats.
Print the distinct values and note they are sorted.
Add return_counts=True to get the frequency of each.
unique removes repeats and sorts.realWorld: A category value-count table — how often each label appears — is unique with counts, not a histogram with hand-made bins.
mistakes: Expecting first-seen order from the output.
Assuming the input was modified.
revision: unique always returns sorted distinct values.
return_counts aligns one count with each unique value.

steps: Find the position of the smallest value.
Fetch the matching row or label with that index.
Check a tie case and confirm the first one wins.
argmin finds the smallest position.realWorld: Locating the worst-performing store or the cheapest supplier is a position question, and the name lookup follows from it.
mistakes: Reading argmin as the minimum value.
Assuming the last occurrence wins on ties.
revision: argmin returns the first position of the minimum.
The value itself comes from min or from indexing.

steps: Compute the order from the sort key.
Index the label array with that order.
Index the key array with the same order and check they agree.
argsort gives positions, sort gives valu.realWorld: Any table sort — customers by revenue, products by margin — is one permutation applied to every column.
mistakes: Sorting names and scores separately, which breaks the pairing.
Reusing a stale order after the data changed.
revision: One argsort, applied to every parallel array, keeps rows aligned.
The permutation is the sort; the values are just one view of it.

steps: Compute the shared values of two arrays.
Compute the union and print it.
Compute the difference and confirm it excludes the shared value.
Set operations on arrays.realWorld: Duplicate detection and list reconciliation are these three calls, and every result is sorted so reports stay stable.
mistakes: Expecting duplicates to survive the operation.
Assuming the order of the inputs is preserved.
revision: All three treat the arrays as sets and return sorted unique values.
setdiff1d is one-way: values in the first that are absent from the second.

steps: Create a view and a copy of the same array.
Write into the view and print the source.
Write into the copy and print the source again.
view shares, copy does not.realWorld: Passing a copy to a helper that mutates its input is the safe choice; passing a view is how the caller's data gets rewritten.
mistakes: Using a[1:] believing it copied.
Copying in every call and doubling memory use.
revision: view shares the buffer; copy allocates a new one.
A write through the view is visible in the source.

steps: Ask whether a slice shares memory with its source.
Ask the same question for a copy.
Print both and read True then False.
Prove sharing with shares_memory.visual:
shares_memory(a, a[1:3]) → True
shares_memory(a, a.copy()) → False
Prove sharing with shares_memory.realWorld: Before mutating a derived array, this is the one check that answers whether the source will change too.
mistakes: Guessing the answer from the operation name.
Assuming the test is cheap on very large arrays — it can be slow.
revision: shares_memory answers the question with a real check.
Slices usually share; copies never do.

steps: Build a (2, 3) int64 matrix.
Print the strides and identify the row and column steps.
Multiply 3 × 8 and confirm it equals the row stride.
Strides describe memory steps.realWorld: Why a transpose is free and why some library calls copy is explained by these two numbers, not by the values.
mistakes: Reading strides as element counts when they are bytes.
Assuming strides are always positive.
revision: Strides are byte offsets per axis step.
C order means the last axis has the smallest stride.

steps: Reshape a contiguous range.
Check sharing with the source.
Write into the reshaped array and confirm the source changed.
reshape usually returns a view.realWorld: A pipeline that reshapes a buffer for a model can avoid a copy only while the layout stays contiguous.
mistakes: Assuming reshape always copies.
Reshaping a transposed array and being surprised by a copy.
revision: Contiguous layouts reshape as views.
A non-contiguous source forces an allocation.

steps: Take a slice of an array.
Print the slice's base.
Confirm the base is the original object.
base points at the source array.visual:
a.base → None
a[1:].base is a → True
base points at the source array.realWorld: When two names mysteriously change together, base is the fastest way to prove they share one buffer.
mistakes: Expecting base to be the immediate slice rather than the owner.
Using base identity where shares_memory is the correct test.
revision: A view's base points at the array that owns the memory.
An owning array reports None.

steps: Print the strides of a matrix.
Print the strides of its transpose.
Confirm the two numbers swapped and no bytes moved.
Transpose is a view with new strides.realWorld: Reorienting a matrix for a solver costs nothing because only the strides change, which is why transposes appear freely in hot loops.
mistakes: Assuming the transpose allocated a new buffer.
Assuming a non-contiguous transpose is still C order.
revision: Transpose swaps strides, not data.
The result is a view and usually not C-contiguous.

steps: Reverse an array with a step of -1.
Print its strides and compare with the source.
Note the only change is the sign.
A reversed slice has negative strides.realWorld: Displaying a sequence backwards at no memory cost is exactly what a negative stride buys.
mistakes: Assuming the reversal copied the data.
Expecting the shape to change.
revision: A negative step negates that axis's stride.
The values stay where they are; only the walk direction changed.

steps: Copy an array.
Read the OWNDATA flag on the copy.
Compare it with the flag on a slice.
copy owns its memory.realWorld: Libraries check OWNDATA to decide whether they may write into an array, and a view fails that test.
mistakes: Assuming OWNDATA on the source tells you anything about a view.
Treating a non-owning array as safe to mutate.
revision: OWNDATA is True only for the array that allocated the buffer.
Views borrow, copies own.

steps: Slice the first two elements.
Write into the slice's first cell.
Print the source to see the write.
A slice is a view into the source.realWorld: In-place block edits rely on this; accidental edits rely on it too, which is why the aliasing is worth naming.
mistakes: Believing a slice allocated memory for itself.
Copying only after the source was already changed.
revision: Basic slicing returns a view of the same buffer.
Nothing was copied when the slice was taken.

steps: Slice and immediately copy the slice.
Write into the copy.
Print the source and confirm it is unchanged.
A copy stops the sharing.realWorld: This is the one-line fix for accidental mutation: copy at the boundary, then work freely.
mistakes: Copying the slice but keeping other aliases of the source.
Assuming copy() also changes the dtype.
revision: copy() allocates a new buffer.
shares_memory is False between a source and its copy.

steps: Print the strides of a (2, 3) matrix.
Explain each number as bytes per step on that axis.
Transpose and print again to see the swap.
Strides describe how memory is walked.realWorld: The difference between a fast and a slow loop over a matrix is usually which axis it walks, and strides are how that is measured.
mistakes: Reading strides as shapes.
Forgetting that a non-contiguous array cannot be flattened for free.
revision: Strides are byte offsets per axis step.
Views only change strides; copies move bytes.

steps: Reshape a contiguous range.
Print the base of the reshaped array.
Transpose, reshape again and see the base change or copy.
A reshape can stay a view.realWorld: Whether a reshape is free decides the memory profile of a preprocessing step that runs on every batch.
mistakes: Assuming every reshape is a view.
Relying on base identity instead of shares_memory.
revision: reshape returns a view when the strides allow.
A transpose or non-contiguous source forces a copy.

steps: Create an int32 and a float64 array of the same length.
Print itemsize and nbytes for both.
Confirm nbytes equals itemsize times size.
itemsize and nbytes.visual:
int32: itemsize 4, nbytes 20
float64: itemsize 8, nbytes 40
itemsize and nbytes.realWorld: Memory budgeting for a batch starts from nbytes; choosing int32 over float64 halves a buffer without changing the shape.
mistakes: Confusing nbytes with the number of elements.
Assuming the shape changed when only the dtype did.
revision: itemsize is bytes per element, nbytes is the whole buffer.
Changing dtype changes both without changing shape.

steps: Print the C flag and strides of a matrix.
Transpose it and print both again.
Explain which axis is walked fastest in each layout.
C order and Fortran order.visual:
a     C True,  strides (24, 8)
a.T   C False, strides (8, 24)
C order and Fortran order.realWorld: An extension that requires C order will copy a transposed input, so the flag explains an otherwise invisible allocation.
mistakes: Assuming any 2-D array is C contiguous.
Ignoring the flag until a copy shows up in profiling.
revision: C order walks the last axis fastest; Fortran order the first.
ascontiguousarray converts to the C layout.
